warmup.q: A ticker emits once per millisecond. Your consumer needs 10 ms per item. You add .onBackpressureBuffer() before it, and the OverflowException you had before goes away. What has really happened?
options: Reactor slowed the ticker down to match the consumer
The extra ticks now wait in an unbounded queue that keeps growing
The extra ticks are dropped, and only the ones the consumer asked for are kept
The consumer now runs on more threads, so it keeps up
warmup.why: onBackpressureBuffer() requests unbounded from the ticker and stores every tick the consumer hasn't asked for yet. Nothing slows the ticker down, and nothing is dropped, so the queue grows by about 90 items per 100 ms for as long as the stream runs. The error went away; the problem became a memory leak. Dropping is what onBackpressureDrop does.

sections.h: Demand is a number that travels up the chain
sections.html:
request(n) is the whole mechanism. A subscriber tells its publisher "I can take n more", the publisher sends at most n, and the subscriber asks again when it is ready. Lesson 1 of this track showed the contract. This lesson is about who sends those numbers in real code, and what happens when a source can't obey them.

Most of the time it isn't you. subscribe(consumer), block() and blockLast() request Long.MAX_VALUE, which the spec treats as unbounded: send everything, as fast as you like. Then each operator between you and the source may change the number on its way up. Put doOnRequest right above an operator and you see what it sends:

Between you and the source The source sees
nothing (blockLast() alone) 9223372036854775807
take(3) 3
limitRate(10) 10, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8
publishOn(single()) 256, 192, 192, 192
flatMap(call, 4) 4, 1, 1, 1, 1
concatMap(call) 1, 1, 1, ...

Operators with a queue inside (publishOn, limitRate, the inner queues of flatMap) prefetch a batch and refill it when about 75% of it has gone out. That keeps the source busy without unbounded buffering.

When you need to control demand yourself, extend BaseSubscriber. Request a first batch in hookOnSubscribe, and more as you finish items:

Java
payments.subscribe(new BaseSubscriber<Payment>() {
    @Override protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription s) { request(2); }
    @Override protected void hookOnNext(Payment p) { post(p); request(1); }
});
Kotlin
payments.subscribe(object : BaseSubscriber<Payment>() {
    override fun hookOnSubscribe(s: Subscription) { request(2) }
    override fun hookOnNext(p: Payment) { post(p); request(1) }
})

Now the part that matters. A source that honours request(n) simply produces less when nobody asks: Flux.range, a database cursor, a paged API client, a Kafka adapter that polls only on demand. Backpressure then works from end to end, and you never have to think about it. A source that can't slow down (a ticker, a WebSocket, a callback API bridged with Flux.create) has to put the extra items somewhere. The third section is about that choice.

try.title: Watch the requests
steps: DemandDemo first runs a BaseSubscriber that asks for 2, then 1 more after each item. Then it puts doOnRequest above five different operators and prints what the source received.
Before running, write down your guess for each of the five lines.
Run it. Then change limitRate(10) to limitRate(10, 0) and predict the new line.

code.title: DemandDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l07; import org.reactivestreams.Subscription; import reactor.core.publisher.BaseSubscriber; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import java.util.function.Function; /** Demand made visible: the requests that reach the source, for one subscriber and five operators. */ public class DemandDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("1. a subscriber that asks for 2, then 1 more after each item"); Flux.range(1, 4) .doOnRequest(n -> System.out.println(" request(" + n + ")")) .subscribe(new BaseSubscriber<Integer>() { @Override protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription s) { request(2); } @Override protected void hookOnNext(Integer item) { System.out.println(" got " + item); request(1); } }); show("2. blockLast() alone", Flux.range(1, 40), f -> f); show("3. take(3)", Flux.range(1, 40), f -> f.take(3)); show("4. limitRate(10)", Flux.range(1, 40), f -> f.limitRate(10)); show("5. publishOn(single())", Flux.range(1, 600), f -> f.publishOn(Schedulers.single())); show("6. flatMap(call, 4)", Flux.range(1, 8), f -> f.flatMap(i -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10)).thenReturn(i), 4)); } static void show(String title, Flux<Integer> source, Function<Flux<Integer>, Flux<Integer>> operator) { List<Long> requests = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); operator.apply(source.doOnRequest(requests::add)).blockLast(); System.out.printf("%-24s the source saw %s%n", title, requests); } }

alt.html: package workbench.reactive.l07 import org.reactivestreams.Subscription import reactor.core.publisher.BaseSubscriber import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList private fun show(title: String, source: Flux<Int>, operator: (Flux<Int>) -> Flux<Int>) { val requests = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Long>() operator(source.doOnRequest { requests += it }).blockLast() println("%-24s the source saw %s".format(title, requests)) } /** Demand made visible: the requests that reach the source, for one subscriber and five operators. */ fun main() { println("1. a subscriber that asks for 2, then 1 more after each item") Flux.range(1, 4) .doOnRequest { n -> println(" request($n)") } .subscribe(object : BaseSubscriber<Int>() { override fun hookOnSubscribe(s: Subscription) { request(2) } override fun hookOnNext(item: Int) { println(" got $item") request(1) } }) show("2. blockLast() alone", Flux.range(1, 40)) { it } show("3. take(3)", Flux.range(1, 40)) { it.take(3) } show("4. limitRate(10)", Flux.range(1, 40)) { it.limitRate(10) } show("5. publishOn(single())", Flux.range(1, 600)) { it.publishOn(Schedulers.single()) } show("6. flatMap(call, 4)", Flux.range(1, 8)) { f -> f.flatMap({ i -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10)).thenReturn(i) }, 4) } }

try.expect: The BaseSubscriber prints request(2), then alternates got n and request(1). The source sees 9223372036854775807 for blockLast() alone, [3] for take(3), [10, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8] for limitRate(10), [256, 192, 192, 192] for publishOn, and [4, 1, 1, 1, 1] for flatMap(call, 4). With limitRate(10, 0) it sees [10, 10, 10, 10, 10]: a new batch only after the last one fully arrived.

sections.h: Use limitRate to turn one big request into small ones
sections.html:
limitRate(n) sits between a subscriber that asks for a lot and a source that should only be asked for a little. It requests n, then tops up by 75% of n each time 75% of the last batch has been delivered. Flux.range(1, 40).limitRate(10) sends 10, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8 upstream. Unlike take, it never cuts the stream short: every item still arrives, in batches.

Use it when the size of the request changes what the source does. A database cursor or a paging client that fetches "as many rows as were requested" will try to fetch the whole table for request(Long.MAX_VALUE). With limitRate(100) in front, the export still streams every row, but never has more than one batch of about 100 in flight:

Java
Flux<LedgerRow> export = cursor.rows(day)
        .limitRate(100)                    // the cursor sees 100, then 75 at a time
        .concatMap(uploader::send);
Kotlin
val export: Flux<LedgerRow> = cursor.rows(day)
    .limitRate(100)                        // the cursor sees 100, then 75 at a time
    .concatMap(uploader::send)

limitRate(highTide, lowTide) sets both numbers. limitRate(10, 0) asks for exactly 10 and waits until all 10 have arrived before asking again (10, 10, 10, 10, 10), which suits an API that works in fixed pages. Its Javadoc says limitRate(n) is equivalent to publishOn(Schedulers.immediate(), n): the same prefetch-and-refill queue, without the thread switch.

Know what it doesn't do. limitRate shapes demand; it doesn't make a slow consumer faster, and it can't help with a source that ignores demand. It also isn't a rate limit in the "per second" sense, despite the name. For that, the last section has a better tool.

sections.h: When the source can't slow down, choose what to lose
sections.html:
Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(1)) ticks once a millisecond, whatever you request. Put a screen behind it that takes 10 ms per tick and asks for one at a time, and the second tick fails the stream: OverflowException: Could not emit tick 1 due to lack of requests. Any source that can't be paused behaves like this, or worse, quietly piles items up: a WebSocket of FX prices, a multicast sink, a callback API.

The onBackpressure operators make the choice explicit. Each one requests unbounded from the source, so the source never overflows, and then decides what to do with the items nobody downstream asked for:

Operator Items with no demand Use it for
onBackpressureBuffer(n) keeps up to n, then cancels the source and fails bursts you must not lose
onBackpressureBuffer() keeps all of them almost nothing: the backlog grows until the heap runs out
onBackpressureDrop(onDropped) drops them, calling onDropped samples, metrics, best-effort events
onBackpressureLatest() keeps only the newest prices, positions, statuses: newer replaces older
onBackpressureError() fails at once cases where falling behind is a bug

Same ticker, same 10 ms screen, 20 frames. Drop showed ticks about 11 apart and threw away about 200. Latest also showed roughly every tenth tick, always the newest one at the moment the screen asked. onBackpressureBuffer(10) delivered ticks 0 to 11 in order, then failed with an overflow error once the buffer was drained. The unbounded buffer delivered 0 to 19 in order, which looks perfect, while the ticker had reached 204: more than 180 ticks were waiting in memory, and that number only grows.

So the name misleads a little. None of these operators slows the source down. They are loss policies: they decide what to keep and what to give up. Real backpressure needs a source that honours request(n). When you have a choice of client or API, pick one that does.

When you bridge a callback API yourself, make the same choice at the bridge: Flux.create(sink -> ..., FluxSink.OverflowStrategy.LATEST). The default strategy of Flux.create is BUFFER, the unbounded one.

try.title: One ticker, five policies
steps: OverflowDemo runs a 1 ms ticker into a screen that asks for one tick at a time and takes 10 ms to draw each. It tries no strategy, then drop, latest, a buffer of 10 and an unbounded buffer, for 20 frames each.
Predict, for each run, which ticks the screen gets and whether it ends with an error.
Run it. For the last run, compare "ticker reached" with the number of ticks the screen got. Where are the others?

code.title: OverflowDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l07; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.function.Function; /** A ticker that can't slow down (one tick per ms) and a screen that needs 10 ms per tick. */ public class OverflowDemo { static void run(String title, Function<Flux<Long>, Flux<Long>> strategy) { AtomicLong produced = new AtomicLong(); List<Long> seen = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); String error = null; try { strategy.apply(Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(1)).doOnNext(produced::set)) .publishOn(Schedulers.single(), 1) // the screen asks for one tick at a time .doOnNext(tick -> sleep(10)) // and takes 10 ms to draw it .take(20) .doOnNext(seen::add) .blockLast(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { error = e.getMessage(); } System.out.printf("%-28s ticker reached %3d, screen got %s%n", title, produced.get(), seen); if (error != null) { System.out.printf("%30sthen the error: %s%n", "", error); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { run("1. no strategy", f -> f); AtomicInteger dropped = new AtomicInteger(); run("2. onBackpressureDrop", f -> f.onBackpressureDrop(tick -> dropped.incrementAndGet())); System.out.printf("%30s(%d ticks dropped)%n", "", dropped.get()); run("3. onBackpressureLatest", Flux::onBackpressureLatest); run("4. onBackpressureBuffer(10)", f -> f.onBackpressureBuffer(10)); run("5. onBackpressureBuffer()", Flux::onBackpressureBuffer); } }

alt.title: OverflowDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.reactive.l07 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong private fun run(title: String, strategy: (Flux<Long>) -> Flux<Long>) { val produced = AtomicLong() val seen = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Long>() var error: String? = null try { strategy(Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(1)).doOnNext(produced::set)) .publishOn(Schedulers.single(), 1) // the screen asks for one tick at a time .doOnNext { Thread.sleep(10) } // and takes 10 ms to draw it .take(20) .doOnNext { seen += it } .blockLast() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { error = e.message } println("%-28s ticker reached %3d, screen got %s".format(title, produced.get(), seen)) if (error != null) println("%30sthen the error: %s".format("", error)) } /** A ticker that can't slow down (one tick per ms) and a screen that needs 10 ms per tick. */ fun main() { run("1. no strategy") { it } val dropped = AtomicInteger() run("2. onBackpressureDrop") { it.onBackpressureDrop { dropped.incrementAndGet() } } println("%30s(%d ticks dropped)".format("", dropped.get())) run("3. onBackpressureLatest") { it.onBackpressureLatest() } run("4. onBackpressureBuffer(10)") { it.onBackpressureBuffer(10) } run("5. onBackpressureBuffer()") { it.onBackpressureBuffer() } }

try.expect: No strategy: the screen gets tick 0, then Could not emit tick 1 due to lack of requests. Drop: about every eleventh tick, with roughly 200 dropped. Latest: about every tenth tick, each the newest at that moment. Buffer of 10: ticks 0 to 11 in order, then The receiver is overrun by more signals than expected. Unbounded buffer: ticks 0 to 19 in order with no error, while the ticker reached about 200. The other 180 or so are sitting in the buffer, and in a long-running service that backlog never stops growing.

sections.h: flatMap's concurrency protects the services you call
sections.html:
Demand also flows from your service toward the services it calls. Each inner publisher in a flatMap is an open request to somebody: the bank's settlement API, Oracle, the fraud service. And flatMap's default concurrency is 256.

In the demo, the bank allows 20 open requests per client and answers in 50 ms. payments.flatMap(this::settle) over 200 payments opens all 200 at once: 20 settle and 180 come back as 429 Too Many Requests. payments.flatMap(this::settle, 20) keeps 20 open at a time, and all 200 settle in about 500 ms: ten rounds of 50 ms. The cap didn't slow down anything the bank would have accepted. It stopped 180 requests that were never going to work.

Java
Flux<Receipt> receipts = payments.flatMap(bank::settle, 20);     // never more than 20 open requests
Kotlin
val receipts: Flux<Receipt> = payments.flatMap(bank::settle, 20) // never more than 20 open requests

The source is backpressured too. flatMap requests 20 payments, subscribes to 20 calls, and requests one more payment each time a call finishes (the 4, 1, 1, 1, 1 pattern from the first section). So a Kafka adapter that polls on demand is never read faster than the bank answers.

Pick the number from the smallest limit on the path, the downstream ceiling from the executors track: the bank's open-request limit, the connection pool, the fraud API's quota. Little's law connects them: 20 open requests of 50 ms each is at most 400 calls per second. A limit of so many calls per second is a different thing, because flatMap caps how many are open, not how many start per second. If the bank also had a per-second quota, you would add a rate limiter as well.

concatMap is the extreme case, concurrency 1. Use flatMapSequential(call, 20) from lesson 3 of this track when you need the results in input order.

try.title: Respect the bank's limit
steps: RateLimitDemo settles 200 payments against a fake bank that allows 20 open requests and refuses the 21st with a 429. Each refused call is skipped with onErrorResume, so the batch keeps going.
Predict both lines: how many settle, how many are refused, and roughly how long each run takes.
Run it. Then change the 20 in the second run to 25 and predict again.

code.title: RateLimitDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l07; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.Function; /** 200 settlement calls against a bank that allows 20 open requests per client. */ public class RateLimitDemo { static final Semaphore openRequests = new Semaphore(20); static final AtomicInteger refused = new AtomicInteger(); // the bank: 50 ms per call, and a 21st concurrent request is refused with a 429 static Mono<String> bankCall(int id) { return Mono.defer(() -> { if (!openRequests.tryAcquire()) { refused.incrementAndGet(); return Mono.error(new IllegalStateException("429 Too Many Requests")); } return Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(50)).map(tick -> { openRequests.release(); // the response frees the slot return "receipt-" + id; }); }); } static void run(String title, Function<Flux<Integer>, Flux<String>> settle) { refused.set(0); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long settled = settle.apply(Flux.range(1, 200)).count().block(); System.out.printf("%-22s %3d settled, %3d refused with 429, in %3d ms%n", title, settled, refused.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } public static void main(String[] args) { bankCall(0).block(); // warm-up, so the timings below are fair // a refused call is skipped, so one 429 doesn't end the whole batch (lesson 5 of this track) run("1. flatMap(call)", f -> f.flatMap(id -> bankCall(id).onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty()))); run("2. flatMap(call, 20)", f -> f.flatMap(id -> bankCall(id).onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty()), 20)); } }

alt.title: RateLimitDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.reactive.l07 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger private val openRequests = Semaphore(20) private val refused = AtomicInteger() // the bank: 50 ms per call, and a 21st concurrent request is refused with a 429 private fun bankCall(id: Int): Mono<String> = Mono.defer { if (!openRequests.tryAcquire()) { refused.incrementAndGet() Mono.error(IllegalStateException("429 Too Many Requests")) } else { Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(50)).map { openRequests.release() // the response frees the slot "receipt-$id" } } } private fun run(title: String, settle: (Flux<Int>) -> Flux<String>) { refused.set(0) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val settled = settle(Flux.range(1, 200)).count().block() println("%-22s %3d settled, %3d refused with 429, in %3d ms".format( title, settled, refused.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } /** 200 settlement calls against a bank that allows 20 open requests per client. */ fun main() { bankCall(0).block() // warm-up, so the timings below are fair // a refused call is skipped, so one 429 doesn't end the whole batch (lesson 5 of this track) run("1. flatMap(call)") { f -> f.flatMap { id -> bankCall(id).onErrorResume { Mono.empty() } } } run("2. flatMap(call, 20)") { f -> f.flatMap({ id -> bankCall(id).onErrorResume { Mono.empty() } }, 20) } }

try.expect: With the default concurrency of 256, all 200 calls open at once: 20 settle and 180 are refused, in well under a second. With a cap of 20, all 200 settle and none are refused, in about 500 ms (ten rounds of 50 ms). With 25, about 5 calls per round are refused, so you lose settlements while gaining nothing: the cap has to match the smallest limit on the path.

analogy: Think of a coffee bar. Real backpressure is the barista taking the next order only when a hand is free: the queue simply waits at the door, which is a source that honours request(n). limitRate is taking orders ten at a time instead of all at once. A source that can't slow down is a conveyor belt of cups that won't stop, and someone has to decide: stack them on a shelf of ten and call the manager when it's full (a bounded buffer that fails), let them fall off (drop), or keep only the last cup (latest). flatMap(call, 20) is a machine with 20 heads: never more than 20 brews at once. The analogy breaks at the shelf. A real shelf that overflows is easy to see. In Reactor, onBackpressureBuffer() with no size is a shelf you can't see, and it grows until the JVM runs out of heap.
world: In payments the loss policy is a business decision, so make it in code where a reviewer can see it. An FX rate feed to a pricing screen wants onBackpressureLatest. Card authorizations and audit events must never be dropped silently, so they get a bounded buffer that fails loudly, plus a way to resume (Kafka offsets, the gateway's last acknowledged id). Metrics samples can be dropped. Calls out of your service are the other half: the issuer, the bank's settlement API and your Oracle pool each have a limit, and flatMap's concurrency should match the smallest of them. Quarkus's Mutiny has the same choices under onOverflow(), and the same reasoning applies.
mistake: The most common mistake is fixing an OverflowException with onBackpressureBuffer() and no size. The error goes away, the tests pass, and in production the buffer quietly holds everything the consumer hasn't caught up with, until a busy morning turns it into an OutOfMemoryError far from the cause. People reach for it because the name sounds like the fix. Decide instead what may be lost: give the buffer a size and a callback (onBackpressureBuffer(10_000, e -> log.error(...))) for data you must keep, onBackpressureLatest for values where newer replaces older, onBackpressureDrop for samples, and prefer a source that honours demand when you have the choice.

compare.title: Loss policies and concurrency caps in Reactor and Kotlin Flow

java.title: Feeds.java (Reactor)
java.html: // Reactor: say what happens when the consumer can't keep up Flux<Tick> screen = ticks.onBackpressureLatest(); // keep only the newest Flux<AuditEvent> audit = events.onBackpressureBuffer(1_000); // hold 1,000, then fail loudly Flux<Receipt> receipts = payments.flatMap(bank::settle, 20); // at most 20 calls in flight

kotlin.title: Feeds.kt (Kotlin Flow)
kotlin.html: // Kotlin Flow: a slow collector suspends the emitter, unless a buffer sits between them val screen: Flow<Tick> = ticks.conflate() // keep only the newest val audit: Flow<AuditEvent> = events.buffer(1_000) // hold 1,000, then the emitter suspends @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) val receipts: Flow<Receipt> = payments.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 20) { p -> flow { emit(bank.settle(p)) } } // at most 20 at once

compare.note: Reactor's backpressure is a number sent upstream with request(n). Kotlin Flow's is suspension: emit() simply doesn't return until the collector is ready, so a cold flow can't overflow and has no demand numbers to reshape. The policies only matter when something puts a buffer between producer and collector: buffer, flowOn, or a hot callbackFlow or SharedFlow. conflate() keeps the newest, like onBackpressureLatest. buffer(1_000) suspends the emitter when full instead of failing, and buffer(n, BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST) or DROP_OLDEST drops. A callback API can't suspend, so inside callbackFlow you call trySend and must handle its failure: that is the place where Flow makes you choose. flatMapMerge(concurrency = 20) is the twin of flatMap(call, 20), and in kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 it still needs an opt-in.

worked.title: Stop a fraud-scoring stream from eating the heap

steps.say: A service receives payment events from a gateway's listener API and scores each one with the fraud service. During the morning peak, heap use climbs for an hour and the pod is killed. The fraud team also reports bursts of 250 concurrent calls from this one client. Find both causes.
steps.code: Flux<PaymentEvent> events = Flux.create(sink -> gateway.onEvent(sink::next)); // push-only listener API events.flatMap(fraud::score) // about 30 ms per call .subscribe(scores::save);

alt.html: val events: Flux<PaymentEvent> = Flux.create { sink -> gateway.onEvent(sink::next) } // push-only listener API events.flatMap(fraud::score) // about 30 ms per call .subscribe(scores::save)

steps.say: Two defaults. Flux.create with no strategy uses BUFFER, which is unbounded: whatever the listener pushes while nobody is asking waits in memory. And flatMap without a number runs up to 256 scoring calls at once. The fraud API allows 50 per client, so most of the extra calls fail, and an error is terminal (lesson 5 of this track), so the stream can die as well as leak.
Make each decision visible. Events must not be lost, but the gateway can replay from an event id, so a bounded buffer that fails is safe. The concurrency comes from the fraud API's limit.
steps.code: Flux.create((FluxSink<PaymentEvent> sink) -> gateway.onEvent(sink::next)) .onBackpressureBuffer(10_000, // 1. a bounded backlog... e -> log.error("backlog full at event {}", e.id())) // ...that says when it overflows .flatMap(fraud::score, 50) // 2. the fraud API's limit, not 256 .subscribe(scores::save, e -> gateway.resumeFrom(lastSavedId())); // 3. on overflow, replay from the last saved event

alt.html: Flux.create { sink: FluxSink<PaymentEvent> -> gateway.onEvent(sink::next) } .onBackpressureBuffer(10_000) { e -> // 1. a bounded backlog... log.error("backlog full at event {}", e.id) } // ...that says when it overflows .flatMap(fraud::score, 50) // 2. the fraud API's limit, not 256 .subscribe(scores::save) { gateway.resumeFrom(lastSavedId()) } // 3. on overflow, replay from the last saved event

steps.say: Now check the size with numbers, not hope. 50 calls in flight at 30 ms each finish at most about 1,666 scores per second (Little's law: 50 / 0.03 s). The morning peak sends 2,000 events per second, so the backlog grows by about 334 per second, and 10,000 slots last about 30 seconds. A burst of a few seconds fits. A peak that lasts an hour doesn't fit any buffer: it needs a faster consumer, more instances, or a source that can be told to wait. A buffer only absorbs bursts; it never fixes a consumer that is slower on average.

lab.title: Four feeds, four backpressure decisions
steps: Run the tests once. All five fail. The tests use TestPublisher.create() as a hot source: it fails with Can't deliver value due to lack of requests when pushed without demand, just like Flux.interval.
For each method in FeedPolicies, answer two questions before writing code: does the source honour request(n), and may anything be lost?
Write each method. Each one is a single operator.
Run the tests until all five pass. Then read settleKeepsTwentyInFlight: it counts calls in flight under virtual time, so the count is exact.
hints: If ledgerExport's first request is 9223372036854775807, nothing between the test and the cursor changed the demand. take(100) would cap the request too, but it stops after 100 rows.
If latestTicks receives 1.0811, you buffered. If it waits and receives 1.0815, you dropped.
If auditEvents holds 1,000 events but never fails, your buffer has no size. onBackpressureError() fails the first audit test instead, because it can't hold anything.
If settle reports 100 calls in flight, you used flatMap without its concurrency argument. If it reports 1, you used concatMap.

drill.title: Score a feed that can't wait
drill.prompt: Close this page. authorizations is a Flux<Authorization> from a WebSocket that cannot slow down. Each one must be scored with fraud.score(a) (returns a Mono<Score>), the fraud API allows 50 calls at once, bursts of up to 5,000 must be absorbed, and nothing may be lost silently: log the authorization that overflows. Write the chain, then compare.

answer.html: Flux<Score> scored = authorizations // a WebSocket feed: it can't slow down .onBackpressureBuffer(5_000, a -> log.error("overflow at {}", a.id())) // hold bursts, fail loudly beyond them .flatMap(fraud::score, 50); // at most 50 calls in flight

alt.html: val scored: Flux<Score> = authorizations // a WebSocket feed: it can't slow down .onBackpressureBuffer(5_000) { a -> log.error("overflow at {}", a.id) } // hold bursts, fail loudly beyond them .flatMap(fraud::score, 50) // at most 50 calls in flight

recap: subscribe(consumer) and block() request Long.MAX_VALUE. Operators reshape that demand on its way up: take(3) asks for 3, flatMap(call, 4) for 4 and then 1 at a time.
limitRate(n) turns a big request into batches of n, topped up by 75%: 10, 8, 8, .... Every item still arrives.
A source that honours request(n) gives you backpressure for free. For one that can't slow down, you must pick a loss policy.
onBackpressureBuffer(n), Drop, Latest and Error all request unbounded upstream. They decide what to keep, not how fast the source goes.
onBackpressureBuffer() with no size hides a backlog until the heap runs out. Give buffers a size and a way to report overflow.
flatMap's concurrency (256 by default) is how many calls you have open at once. Set it from the smallest downstream limit.

explain.prompt: A teammate got OverflowException: Could not emit tick ... due to lack of requests and wants to add onBackpressureBuffer() because "that's what backpressure is for". Explain what backpressure really is in Reactor, why their fix is risky, and what you would ask before choosing a fix.
explain.answer: Backpressure is the subscriber telling the source how many items it can take, with request(n), and the source sending no more than that. A source like Flux.interval can't wait, so when the consumer falls behind, it fails instead of slowing down. onBackpressureBuffer() with no size doesn't slow anything either: it asks the source for everything and keeps every item the consumer hasn't asked for in an unbounded queue. The error disappears, and the backlog grows until memory runs out. Before choosing, I'd ask two things: can we use a source that honours demand instead, and if not, what may we lose? If old values are useless, keep the latest. If samples are fine to skip, drop them and count the drops. If nothing may be lost, use a bounded buffer that fails loudly and a way to resume, and check with Little's law that the consumer is fast enough on average, because a buffer only absorbs bursts.

deeper.html:
Sources that pull. Flux.generate calls your generator once per requested item, so it is backpressured by construction: good for paging through an API or reading a file line by line. Flux.create gives you a FluxSink for push APIs, and sink.onRequest(n -> ...) lets you pull n items from an API that supports it, which turns a push bridge into a real backpressured source.

More buffer options. onBackpressureBuffer(maxSize, onOverflow, BufferOverflowStrategy.DROP_OLDEST) keeps the buffer bounded but evicts old items instead of failing (DROP_LATEST and ERROR are the other strategies). onBackpressureBuffer(Duration ttl, int maxSize, onEvicted) also evicts items older than the ttl, for data that goes stale.

Prefetch everywhere. Many operators take a prefetch argument: flatMap(fn, concurrency, prefetch) sets how many items each inner is asked for (32 by default), concatMap(fn, prefetch) and publishOn(scheduler, prefetch) likewise. Smaller numbers mean less memory and more request round trips.

Demand across the network. Reactive Streams demand stops at the process boundary. RSocket carries request(n) across the wire. HTTP has no request(n) of its own: a server streaming to a slow client relies on TCP flow control, and it is the server library's job to turn a full socket into lower demand on your Flux.

Deprecated name. limitRequest(n) is deprecated in favour of take(n), which in 3.8 caps the upstream request at n by default.
